headline: Older adults took more steps on days with younger family

sources.title: The Journals of Gerontology: Series B

chunks.text: Many people {{slow down}} as they get older. A new study adds a detail. Researchers at Stanford University and Washington University in St. Louis {{carried out}} the study with 265 [[participants]], aged 23 to 92. On days when older adults spent more time with younger [[relatives]], they took more steps. They also reported more [[high-energy]] positive feelings, such as happiness, [[enthusiasm]] and excitement. The study was published in The Journals of Gerontology, Series B, on September 10, 2026.

verbs.correct: To become less active than before
verbs.wrong: To learn a new skill quickly
verbs.why: A busy lawyer slows down after retirement, and a puppy slows down once it is a few years old. Many people slow down as they get older, which is why the study looked at what older adults did each day.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To continue after a difficult time
verbs.why: A mechanic carries out repairs on a car, and a school carries out a fire drill twice a year. Researchers at two universities carried out the study with 265 participants aged 23 to 92.

chunks.text: Each person kept a [[daily diary]] for nine days. Each day, they {{filled in}} a short record of who they spent time with and how they felt. The researchers did not leave [[physical activity]] to memory. Instead, they {{kept track of}} it [[objectively]], through [[step count]] and the number of minutes each person spent sitting. The diaries and the movement data were then placed [[side by side]] to see whether the two moved together.

verbs.correct: To complete a form with information
verbs.wrong: To sign a paper to join a study
verbs.why: A traveler fills in a customs form at the airport, and a patient fills in a health history at the clinic. Each day, the participants filled in a short record of who they spent time with and how they felt.

verbs.correct: To record and follow something over time
verbs.wrong: To stay at the same level as others
verbs.why: A parent keeps track of a child's height on the kitchen wall, and a driver keeps track of fuel costs in a notebook. The researchers kept track of physical activity through step counts and minutes spent sitting.

chunks.text: Older adults were not the only ones who felt better. Across every age in the study, one part of the [[pattern]] {{held up}}. On days with more time with younger family members, people reported more calm positive feelings, such as [[contentment]] and [[relaxation]], as they {{wound down}} before bed. The same link did not {{show up}} for other company. Time spent with people who were not younger family members had no [[connection]] to step count or [[sitting time]].

verbs.wrong: To keep something in a safe place
verbs.why: A weather forecast holds up if the rain arrives as promised, and an alibi holds up if the times match the facts. The calm feelings before bed held up across every age in the study, not only among older adults.

verbs.correct: To relax before going to sleep
verbs.wrong: To visit family for a short stay
verbs.why: Some people wind down with a warm bath, and others wind down by listening to a podcast in the dark. Participants reported more contentment and relaxation as they wound down on days with more time with younger family members.
A stain shows up on a white shirt, and a typing error shows up when you print the page. The link with step counts did not show up for time spent with people who were not younger family members.

chunks.text: It is important to {{point out}} that the study found a link, not a [[cause]]. Nine days of diaries do not {{add up to}} [[proof]]. The study cannot {{rule out}} other [[explanations]]. The results do not show that a visit {{cheers up}} an older person. They show only that family days and active days were often the same days. Even so, the pattern raises a question for [[future studies]]. What happens when the [[generations]] {{get together}}, or simply {{hang out}} at home?

verbs.correct: To tell people about a fact
verbs.wrong: To give something to each person
verbs.why: A guide points out that the museum is free on Sundays, and a friend points out that your shirt is on backwards. It is important to point out that the study found a link, not a cause.

verbs.correct: To combine to produce a result
verbs.why: Three short walks add up to an hour of exercise, and a few missed classes add up to a low grade. Nine days of diaries do not add up to proof that family time causes anything.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.why: A vet rules out a broken bone after an X-ray, and a coach rules out an injured player for the final. The study cannot rule out other explanations for why family days and active days often matched.

verbs.wrong: To live near a family member
verbs.why: A sunny morning cheers up the whole office, and a funny movie cheers up a friend after a bad week. The results do not show that a visit from a younger relative cheers up an older person.

verbs.wrong: To reach the end of a hard time
verbs.why: Neighbors get together for a barbecue in July, and former coworkers get together once a year for lunch. The study raises the question of what happens when the generations get together.

verbs.correct: To spend relaxed time with someone
verbs.wrong: To wait for a short time
verbs.why: College friends hang out in the dorm on Friday nights, and cousins hang out by the pool all summer. Older adults took more steps on days when they spent time with, or simply hung out with, younger family members.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day diary study found that older adults took more steps and felt happier on days spent with younger family members. The study shows a link, not a cause.
mainIdea.why: Researchers tracked 265 people with diaries and objective activity measures, and older adults moved more and felt better on days with more time with younger relatives, though the study cannot rule out other explanations.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day diary study found that older adults took more steps and felt happier on days spent with anyone at all. Friends and neighbors had the same effect as family.
mainIdea.why: Close, but time spent with people who were not younger family members showed no connection to step count or sitting time.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day walking program helped older adults sleep better and feel calmer at night, according to a new study. The program is now being tested in several cities.
mainIdea.why: The study did not test a walking program at all; it tracked what people did and felt day by day and found a link between family time and activity.

tf.s: The researchers kept track of activity with step counts and sitting time.
tf.why: Physical activity was measured objectively, by step count and by the minutes each person spent sitting, rather than from memory.

tf.s: The participants filled in a daily diary for nine weeks.
tf.why: Each person filled in a daily diary for nine days, not nine weeks.

tf.s: Calm feelings before bed held up across every age in the study.
tf.why: People of all ages reported more contentment and relaxation as they wound down on days with more time with younger family members.

tf.s: Time with people who were not younger relatives also showed up in the step data.
tf.why: The link did not show up for other company, because time with people who were not younger family members had no connection to step count or sitting time.

tf.s: The study found a link between family time and steps, not a cause.
tf.why: Nine days of diaries do not add up to proof, and the study cannot rule out other explanations.

tf.s: The study proved that visits from younger relatives cheer up older adults.
tf.why: The results do not show that a visit cheers up an older person; they show only that family days and active days were often the same days.

lines.text: Did you see the study about older adults and their younger relatives?
The one with the step counts? My mother would love that.
That's the one. Researchers {{carried out}} a nine-day diary study with 265 people.
How does a diary tell you how much someone walked?
It doesn't. They {{kept track of}} steps and sitting time with devices, so nobody had to guess.
So on days they {{hung out}} with younger family, the older people moved more?
More steps, and they felt happier and more excited too.
A three-year-old will [[keep you on your toes]]. You can't sit still with a toddler in the house.
Maybe. But the study can't {{rule out}} other explanations.
Like people who already felt good chose to {{get together}}?
Exactly. [[Which came first?]] Nobody knows yet.
Did anything {{hold up}} for younger people too?
One thing did. Everyone felt calmer as they {{wound down}} before bed on those days.
It didn't {{show up}} in the step data at all.
Interesting. Still, nine days isn't very long.
True. It's a link, not a cause. But [[it can't hurt]]. It's [[worth a phone call]] to your mother.

expressions.def: To keep someone busy, alert and ready to act all the time
ex: A new puppy will keep you on your toes.
Twins keep their parents on their toes all day.

expressions.def: Asked when two things are connected but it is not clear which one causes the other.
ex: Happy people exercise more, or exercise makes people happy. Which came first?

expressions.def: Used to say that something is worth doing because there is no risk in trying
ex: Ask for a discount. It can't hurt.
Drink more water. It can't hurt.

expressions.def: A good enough reason to call someone.
ex: The job may not be perfect, but it's worth a phone call.
Grandma's birthday is worth a phone call at least.
